sources.scope: EPO; gear/flag/grid catch data and purse-seine billfish measurements
sources.outcome: Public catalogue reviewed via web search; raw HTTP retrieval403. Tuna catch tables do not supply length bins. Billfish observer measurements apply to purse-seine vessels, not all gear or HS077 catch. No HS077 all-fleet catch-mass split established.

sources.scope: EPO tuna fisheries, size composition Section5
sources.outcome: Opened via web tool; direct PDF HTTP403. Length sampling informs landed-fish composition; distributions separated by gear/set. Report-wide EPO frequency material does not supply HS077 all-fleet 2019 mass fractions at exact model cutoffs. Could inform future spatial/fleet raising, but not defensibly substituted as observed regional weights.

sources.scope: Stock assessment size inputs and survey size standardization
sources.outcome: Primary search text shows2cm bins and fishery-specific catch composition; survey length data instead represent abundance and receive catch-rate raising. No HS077 matched all-fleet mass allocation recovered; cannot combine raw counts or survey composition directly.

sources.scope: Former public size data endpoint
sources.outcome: HTTP404; followed current official endpoint below.

sources.scope: WCPO aggregated size/length data and metadata
sources.outcome: HTTP200; retained HTML. Download requires registration and no dataset link exposed. No account created or registration submitted. Relevant data exist, but their regional/gear sampling, units, coverage and mass fractions could not be inspected in this run.

sources.scope: SPC official size-composition submission schema
sources.outcome: Records are fish counts by length/weight class, gear, flag, fleet, time and spatial cell; schema is not a catch-mass share dataset. Would require sampling/raising checks and conversion before allocation.

sources.scope: 1950-2024 fishery catch/effort at1degree or5degree resolution
sources.outcome: Catch/effort data can support fleet weighting but does not establish caught-fish size fractions alone. Regional/year length data and consistent sampling expansion still required.

sources.scope: Kiribati national fleet and coastal-state reporting
sources.outcome: Downloaded1453250-byte PDF and extracted text;26pages. Reports catch/effort and port sampling programme; no usable regional catch-at-length mass table at43/120/124cm found. National fleet reporting is not equivalent to Gilbert Islands EEZ catch.

sources.scope: PNG national and coastal-state fishery reporting
sources.outcome: Downloaded PDF and extracted text;32pages. Operational/observer/port sampling coverage and catches found; no usable EEZ catch-at-length mass table at43/120/124cm found. Coverage counts alone do not supply stage shares.

online_search.decision: No directly usable observed regional catch-mass fractions recovered after targeted primary-source search. Proceed with explicitly assumed historical model-catch proxy; preserve infant-missing/assumed-zero distinction and source/model limitations. This is not a claim that size data do not exist.

proposals.definition: Exact source counterpart stage groups; Juv. hake: Appendix B: Juvenile Hake. Biomass for juvenile hake (Merluccius productus) was solved for by the model (assuming an EE value of 0.8) since this group was mainly included to be prey for multiple predator species, including adult hake. This group is meant to represent biomass of age 0 and 1 juvenile hake. PB and QB values were taken from other Ecopath models in nearby systems (Ainsworth et al. 2002; Aydin et al. 2007). We found a range of potential values for both, PB = 1.061-2.67 and QB = 5.31-6.98, and taking these ranges to be the 5th and 95th percentiles, we found the mean of the range based on a lognormal distribution. This led to a PB of 1.75 and a QB of 6.1. Diet for juvenile hake came from two different Buckley data sets: Buckley et al. 1999 and unpublished Buckley diet data (T.W. Buckley, unpublished data) for hake for multiple size classes. Using only predator sizes of 20 cm or less, we calculated a diet of 0.2% amphipods, 0.6% epibenthic fauna, 8% copepods, 80% euphuasiids, 1.4% carnivorous zooplankton, 1.4% benthic shrimp, 6% mesopelagic fish, 0.1% cephalopods, 1% juvenile hake (cannibalism), and 0.5% herring.
proposals.limitations: Existing mapping preserved bit-for-bit. Source zero juvenile catch is a model selectivity proxy, not observed regional stage composition.

zero_catch_juvenile_candidates.definition: Appendix B: Juvenile Rockfish. This groups consists of juveniles of any and all rockfish species in the California Current, where juveniles are approximately ages 0-2 or the size that can be consumed by a seabird. Production and consumption values were borrowed from Field (2004). Diet was also taken from Field (2004). Biomass was solved for in the model through top-down balancing, using an EE of 0.8.

Appendix B: Juvenile Hake. Biomass for juvenile hake (Merluccius productus) was solved for by the model (assuming an EE value of 0.8) since this group was mainly included to be prey for multiple predator species, including adult hake. This group is meant to represent biomass of age 0 and 1 juvenile hake. PB and QB values were taken from other Ecopath models in nearby systems (Ainsworth et al. 2002; Aydin et al. 2007). We found a range of potential values for both, PB = 1.061-2.67 and QB = 5.31-6.98, and taking these ranges to be the 5th and 95th percentiles, we found the mean of the range based on a lognormal distribution. This led to a PB of 1.75 and a QB of 6.1. Diet for juvenile hake came from two different Buckley data sets: Buckley et al. 1999 and unpublished Buckley diet data (T.W. Buckley, unpublished data) for hake for multiple size classes. Using only predator sizes of 20 cm or less, we calculated a diet of 0.2% amphipods, 0.6% epibenthic fauna, 8% copepods, 80% euphuasiids, 1.4% carnivorous zooplankton, 1.4% benthic shrimp, 6% mesopelagic fish, 0.1% cephalopods, 1% juvenile hake (cannibalism), and 0.5% herring.

Appendix B: Juvenile Flatfish. This includes juvenile life stages of starry flounder (Platichthys stellatus), Pacific sanddab (Citharichthys sordidus), Slender sole (Lyopsetta exilis), Pacific sand sole (Psettichthys melanostictus), Butter sole (Isopsetta isolepis), Rock sole (Lepidopsetta bilineata), English sole (Parophrys vetulus), Petrale sole (Eopsetta jordani), Dover sole (Microstomus pacificus), Rex sole (Glyptocephalus zachirus), and any other Pleuronectiformes species. This group was borrowed from the Field (2004) model. PB, QB, EE, and diet were all borrowed from Field (2004) and biomass was solved for in the model based on top-down balancing.

Appendix B: Juvenile Roundfish. This group includes juvenile life stage of sablefish (Anoplopoma fimbria) and lingcod (Ophiodon elongatus) species. This group was borrowed from the Field (2004) model. PB, QB, and EE were all borrowed from Field (2004) and biomass was solved for in the model based on top-down balancing. Diet was borrowed from Field (2004) with a few adjustments for the new forage fish groups. Using the diet from Field (2004) and information from the diet study by Brodeur et al. (1987) on consumption of specific forage fish, the diet became: 1.1% amphipods, 81.8% copepods, 12.3% euphasusiids, 2.9% macrozooplankton, 0.1% anchovy, 0.1% herring, 0.1% sandlance, 0.5% whitebait smelt, and 1.1% saury.

Appendix B: Juvenile Thornyhead. This group included juvenile ages of shortspine and longspine thornyhead species (Sebastolobus). This group was borrowed from the Field (2004) model. PB, QB, EE, and diet were all borrowed from Field (2004) and biomass was solved for in the model based on top-down balancing.

Appendix B: JUVENILE northern elephant seals. Juvenile Northern elephant seals (Mirounga angustirostris) and adult elephant seals were split into two groups because each has quite different migration patterns. Again, instead of adjusting for absence from the system in the biomass parameter, input consumption was added to the diet to represent the amount of prey that both these groups are consuming when not in the system and thus reflecting migration. All things considered, there biomass values are related to each other, which is understandable.
